spec.title: PROP-066 — Remap: replaceable artifact sources for closed networks, shared as packages

status.comment: Drafted 2026-10-31 on the owner's request; awaiting the owner's reading before implementation.

p.purpose: A vibe installation must work where the public hosts are unreachable, filtered, or forbidden by policy: no internet, a corporate network that allows one artifact store, a security team that names the only places bytes may come from. Every artifact vibe fetches gets a replaceable source, the replacement is declared once as data, and the declaration travels between people as an ordinary package. The failure this avoids is the one the owner met in NixOS: everything nailed to one public host, with no layer in between to point elsewhere.

p.principle: Identity is content, location is a replaceable detail. Everything vibe downloads already carries a hash (`vibe.lock` `content_hash`, `sha256` of application inputs, the publisher's digest in `DISTRIBUTIONS.json`, `content_hash` of embedded sources). A remap changes only where bytes are looked for; the bytes are verified against the same hash as before, so a remap can make a fetch fail or succeed but never change what is installed. Different bytes need a new capture and review, never a fallback that accepts them (`campaigns/next` R-027).

p.row: A remap is one `[[remap]]` row with three parts. **What** it matches, exactly one of: `sha256 = "<hex>"` (any artifact declared with that digest, whatever its URL); `package = "<group>/<name>[@<req>]"` (the registry package, its index entries and its embedded sources); `registry = "<name>"` (every URL a declared registry resolves to, including its index and raw-file endpoints); `prefix = "<url prefix>"` (every URL starting with it, the host rewrite). **With** what, exactly one of: `url = "…"` (an `https://`, `http://`, `file://` or git URL; for `prefix` the matched prefix is replaced by it, for the other keys it is the whole new location), `path = "…"` (a local file or directory; a directory is searched as `<path>/<sha256>/<filename>` the way the application download cache is laid out), or `deny = true` (the fetch is refused before any connection, naming the row). **Where** it applies, optional: `scope = { package = "…" }` or `scope = { package = "…", step = "ID" }` limits a row to the installation of one application package or one of its steps. Every row may carry `reason`, shown by `explain` and in refusals; a package carrying rows may describe the whole offer in `[remap] description = "…"` (what network this is for, who maintains it, where to ask), and that text heads every question and listing about it.

p.diagnostics: Being sent to another address is suspicious by nature, so every place a remap is shown says what a reader needs to judge it, computed, never trusted from the package: the target host and scheme (`https`, plain `http` marked `unencrypted`, `file://` and `path` marked `local`, git over ssh marked by its host), whether the host is a private address or a public one, how many of the package's rows point at each host, which rows are `deny`, which rows widen scope (a `prefix` row over a public host is marked `broad`), and whether the target answered a `HEAD` the last time `remap test` ran. A row whose target cannot be classified is shown as `unknown`, not hidden. `explain` adds, for one fetch, the full chain: declared origin, every matching row in winning order with its package, layer and reason, the chosen target, and the digest that will be checked.

p.precedence: When several rows match one fetch the most specific key wins: `sha256`, then `package`, then `registry`, then `prefix` (the longest prefix among prefixes). A scoped row beats an unscoped row of the same key. Among equally specific rows the one from the higher layer of `#layers` wins, and inside one layer the later row. `vibe remap explain <url|sha256>` prints every matching row in winning order with its set and layer, so a surprising choice is one command away.

p.layers: Rows come from four layers, lowest first: remap packages the user has accepted in the user home (`#consent`); remap packages the project requires in `vibe.toml` (`[requires.remaps]`, resolved and locked like any dependency so every clone of the project sees the same offer, applied on each machine only after that user's acceptance); local rows in `.vibe/settings.local.toml` and `~/.vibe/settings.toml` (`[[remap]]` tables, for one developer's machine, no acceptance needed because the user wrote them); and the invocation, `--remap <file.toml>` (repeatable) or `VIBE_REMAP=<file>[,<file>]`. The existing registry `[[mirror]]` and `[[override]]` tables of PROP-002 stay as they are and are read as rows of the local layer (`registry = …` and `package = …` respectively), so nothing a user wrote stops working.

p.package: Any vibepack may carry `[[remap]]` rows and an optional `[policy]` table; a package whose manifest declares `[package] kind = "remap"` carries nothing else and nothing executable. Either way the rows are an **offer**, never an obligation: installing the package records the offer and applies no row until the user accepts it (`#consent`). A remap package is versioned, content-hashed, published to any registry (an internal one included), installed with `vibe install -g` into the user home or required by a project, listed by `vibe list -g`, and removable like any package. Several accepted packages are read in their acceptance order unless a package declares `priority = N` (higher wins among packages). This is how a colleague's or an architect's list reaches a team: publish it, require it, or hand it over on a disk; each person then decides whether their machine follows it.

p.consent: Acceptance is per user home and bound to the package's content hash: `vibe remap accept <package>` records it, `vibe remap reject <package>` records the refusal so the question is not asked again, and a new version of an accepted package is a new offer. **The default is always a question.** When a run would apply an offer that is neither accepted nor rejected, an attended terminal shows the package, its reason, every row it carries (what each one redirects and to where, and what it denies) and asks `apply? [y/N]`; an unattended run (`--json`, no terminal, `--yes` absent) refuses with `consent_required`, naming `vibe remap accept <package>`. The flags: `--accept-remap` (install, update and every verb that resolves artifacts) accepts every offer the run meets, `--accept-remap <package>` (repeatable) accepts named ones, `--reject-remap` rejects every unasked offer for this run without recording anything; `vibe install -g <remap package> --accept-remap` installs and accepts in one go. An offer that is rejected or still unanswered is listed by `vibe remap list` as `offered` or `rejected`, and `vibe remap enable|disable` switches an accepted package off and on without removing it or forgetting the acceptance. A graphical client gets the same question through the `consent_required` envelope and answers it with `accept`.

p.providers: The home keeps a map of its active rows: for every row the packages that offer it (`<home>/remap/providers.json`, derived from the installed packages and the acceptance ledger `<home>/remap/consent.json`, rebuilt whenever either changes, never the sole home of a fact). Two rows are the same when key, target and scope are equal. `vibe remap list` shows each row with its providers, so a row many accepted packages share reads differently from one a single package brought. The map is what uninstall consults.

p.uninstall: Uninstalling a package that offers accepted rows never silently changes what the machine fetches from. Before removing, vibe shows the rows that would stop applying (those with no other accepted provider), the rows that stay because another package still offers them, and asks `keep these N rows as local rows? [Y/n]`: `yes` copies the orphaned rows into the user home's local layer with `from = "<package>@<version>"` and the original reason, so the machine keeps working and `list` still says where each row came from; `no` drops them. The flags `--keep-remap` and `--drop-remap` answer without asking; unattended runs without a flag refuse with `consent_required` the same way acceptance does. The acceptance record itself is deleted with the package.

p.display: Every human view of remaps is one layout, aligned the way `PROP-065#plan` aligns a plan: a header block (package key and version, `description`, registry it came from, state), one numbered block per row (`N. <key kind> <what>` on the first line, then indented `to <target> [<scheme>, <private|public|local>]`, `why <reason>`, `scope …` and `from …` when present, and a `note` line for `unencrypted`, `broad` or `unknown`), and a footer summarising targets per host (`3 rows → nexus.corp.example (https, private); 1 row → local path; 1 deny`). The consent question, `list`, `explain`, the uninstall question and the `--json` documents all carry the same fields in the same order, so a graphical client renders the same blocks. Nothing is abbreviated to fit: long targets wrap under their label, and `--json` is the escape for machines.

p.policy: `[policy] unmatched = "allow" | "deny"` in a remap package or a local layer: with `deny`, any fetch no row matches is refused before a connection, naming the URL, the hash and the sets consulted. The strictest policy of all active layers applies. `vibe remap test` walks a project's or a home's declared artifacts (lock entries, application inputs of installed packages, the distribution manifest) and reports which row each one resolves to and whether the target answers a `HEAD`, without downloading, so a policy can be checked before it bites.

p.locator: One resolution point in `vibe-core` (`Locator`) is the only way a crate turns a declared source into the places to try. Its input is the artifact's identity (kind, declared URL or git locator, digest when declared, the package and step it belongs to); its output is the ordered candidate list with the winning row attached, or a `deny` refusal. Every fetch path adopts it: registry clones, redirects and git-source dependencies (PROP-002), the index and raw-file endpoints (PROP-005; the hardcoded `raw.githubusercontent.com` and `gitverse.ru` table becomes the default rows), embedded sources (PROP-021; the cache key becomes the content hash so the same bytes from another host hit), application inputs of `sources`, `archive` and `native` steps (PROP-059, PROP-065; `archive` and `native` inputs gain the same `<sha256>` cross-run cache `sources` have), `vibe self` distributions (PROP-019: the release base and the `DISTRIBUTIONS.json` location become remappable and the check that refused a non-GitHub base is dropped; the source-install mirror list accepts a remapped clone URL), the documentation shell (PROP-057), and the install scripts (`VIBEVM_RELEASE_ORIGIN` honoured, not only declared). The one `[proxy]` table (`https`, `http`, `no_proxy`) in settings reaches reqwest and child `git` through the same point.

p.not-covered: What a recipe script does on its own (`curl`, `git clone`, `pip install` inside a `recipe` step) is outside vibe's fetches and outside this PROP. Such a step declares `needs = "network"` (PROP-065), and under a `deny` policy the plan marks it `needs network, not remappable` so the reader sees it before the build starts. The recommended package shape in a closed network is to declare such downloads as `[[sources]]` inputs with digests, which this PROP then covers.

p.provenance: Where bytes came from is recorded beside what they are: `vibe.lock` package rows gain `fetched_from` (URL actually used) next to the canonical `source_url`; application run records and `steps.json` record per input the candidate that served it and the row that chose it; the install record of `vibe self` names the base used. `--json` reports carry the same fields. Nothing in a manifest or a lock is rewritten to the remapped URL, so a lock stays portable between networks and the canonical origin stays visible for review.

p.transport: Getting the first set into a closed network: `vibe remap export <package> --out <dir> [--with-artifacts]` writes a `file://` registry holding the remap package and, with `--with-artifacts`, every artifact its rows and the current project's lock name, laid out by digest; `vibe remap import <dir>` (or plain `vibe install -g --registry <dir> <package>`) installs from it, and `vibe cache import <dir>` places the artifacts into the machine store and the application download cache by their digests, verifying each. The existing `vibe registry vendor` stays the way to vendor registry packages; `export --with-artifacts` calls it.

p.commands: `vibe remap list [--json]` (packages by layer with their state `offered` / `accepted` / `rejected` / `disabled`, local rows, policy); `explain <url|sha256> [--json]`; `test [--json]`; `accept|reject <package>`; `enable|disable <package>`; `export`; `import`. The JSON forms are the `vibe-remap/1` documents and are the only interface a graphical client needs: a remap package shows as an installed package with its state and a switch, an unanswered offer shows as a question with its rows, `explain` answers a hover, `test` fills a readiness panel, and the provenance fields of a run record show which row served each download of an installation.

p.acceptance: Public Linux fixtures: a remap package with one row of each key installed into a scratch home and applied only after `remap accept` (an install without acceptance and without a terminal refuses with `consent_required`; `--accept-remap` on the install accepts it; a rejected package is not asked about again), a registry package resolved through a `prefix` row to a `file://` mirror with the lock recording `fetched_from`; an application `sources` input served by a `sha256` row from a directory, the same input refused by a `deny` row with the row named; a `scope.step` row applying to one step and not another; `unmatched = "deny"` refusing an unlisted URL before any connection (the test server counts zero hits); `explain` listing two competing rows in the right order; `export --with-artifacts` then `import` and `cache import` into a second scratch home followed by an `--offline` install that succeeds; a remapped `vibe self bootstrap --release-base` accepted. MT-07 on a host with networking cut: install an application and update vibe through a remap package served from a directory.

p.decisions: Decision: remaps are data rows keyed by digest, package, registry or prefix, carried by an installable package, resolved at one point, verified by the unchanged digests. Why: digests already exist for everything fetched; a package is the one unit vibe already versions, hashes, publishes, installs and lists, so sharing and the graphical client come for free. A remap is an offer a user accepts, because a package author must not be able to redirect another person's downloads by being installed. Rejected: environment variables per host (they cannot be shared or reviewed and they leak); rewriting URLs inside manifests or locks (loses provenance, breaks portability between networks); a fallback that accepts a mirror's different bytes (the Nix lesson, and R-027); a remap package that other packages may depend on (policy belongs to the user and the project, never to a dependency). Open for the owner: whether `[proxy]` belongs in a remap package as well as in settings, and whether a project may forbid user-home packages from applying (`[remap] project_only = true`).

p.supersedes: PROP-002 `TRUST-MIRROR-HATCH` (`--trust-mirror`, specified and never shipped) is withdrawn: no flag accepts a mirror's different bytes. PROP-002 `vibe list --overrides` (specified, never shipped) is replaced by `vibe remap list`, which shows the `[[override]]` and `[[mirror]]` rows as the local layer. PROP-002's tables themselves stay; this PROP adds keys to them and a resolution point above them.

p.client: For a graphical client the whole surface is: `remap list --json` for the catalog of packages and rows with their states and diagnostics; the `consent_required` envelope as the question, answered with `remap accept` or `remap reject`; `remap explain --json` for a hover on any download of a plan or a run record; `remap test --json` for a readiness panel; `uninstall` of a providing package answered with `--keep-remap` or `--drop-remap` after the client shows the orphaned rows. The client never reads or writes `consent.json`, `providers.json` or any TOML of the layers.

p.changelog: 2026-10-31 — drafted; renamed from substitutions to remap; consent, diagnostics, providers, uninstall, display and client surface added; PROP-002 tails marked.
